summary: Belle Isle South End Lower Light, on a cliff at the south end of Belle Isle in the Strait of Belle Isle: lit 1878-79, rebuilt 1908 on a concrete base, still shown.

structures.type: concrete base with masonry wall, red metal lantern topped with dome
structures.note: Register calls it a lantern with no tower. The Coast Guard list describes a 'square skeleton tower, red and white rectangular daymark'. Sources disagree; flagged.

access.note: Grounds open, tower closed (Lighthouse Friends). Remote island, best seen by boat or from the air. Light sits on a cliff with no secure life-line (Lighthouse Friends, 1960s-era account).

events.note: First (upper) light on the south end of the island, first lit 15 March 1858. Built by the Province of Canada. Lower light is a separate later tower on the same station.
Lightning struck the tower and dwelling on the night of 9 August 1876; keeper Martin Coltin and a family member seriously injured. Lightning rods added that autumn (Lighthouse Friends).

Second (lower) light established 300 feet (91 m) lower than the old light; wooden pyramidal building, fixed catoptric light at 160 ft (49 m). Parks Canada statement, as reproduced by the Register, says the wooden lower light dated from 1878.
Rocket fog signal put into service at the station, chosen after a comparison of signals in 1890.
First-class fog signal, first-order double sirens, commenced operation 9 September 1899, cost $20,112.64 (Lighthouse Friends).
Wooden lower tower dismantled and replaced.

Built in 1908 to replace the wooden lower lighthouse: concrete base with masonry wall and red metal lantern (Register). Lighthouse Friends: a new circular metal lantern placed on the old foundation, raised three feet.
Second-order Fresnel lens; occulting white light visible five seconds, dark five seconds; petroleum vapour under an incandescent mantle (Lighthouse Friends).
Fog alarm relocated to the upper lighthouse.
Radio direction-finding station established near the lighthouse; by 1958 the light station ran on its electricity.
Fire in the fog alarm building in March 1969 while keepers were stripping its floor; three keepers injured (Lighthouse Friends).
Lower, upper and keepers' duplex declared Recognized Federal Heritage Buildings (Lighthouse Friends).
Station de-staffed; upper and lower lights remain active (Lighthouse Friends).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Lighthouse Friends gives 1879 for the second light's establishment. The Parks Canada statement, as reproduced by the Register, says the wooden lower light dated from 1878. Not resolved; the story gives 1878 or 1879 as the sources state. The record's first_lit 1879 follows Lighthouse Friends and the Coast Guard's own record.

The station record gives 1908 for the present structure, which matches both the Register and Lighthouse Friends. The Coast Guard list describes a square skeleton tower; the Register says there is no tower. Not resolved.

Lighthouse Friends says the lower light was declared a Recognized Federal Heritage Building in 1990. The station record gives a later heritage lighthouse designation (2015, not checked against a page I read). Both can be true as separate statuses.

The 1908 description (Lighthouse Friends) gives an occulting light, five seconds visible and five dark. The Coast Guard list now gives Fl W 20s (1 s flash, 19 s eclipse). The change is undated in the sources.

The Coast Guard list (51 52 38.0 N, 055 23 03.0 W) and Lighthouse Friends give 51.877222, -55.384167 (the record's position). The station record's conflict list gives a Parks Canada position of 51.88669, -55.39501, about 1.3 km away; that Parks record was not read here. Not resolved; the record keeps the Coast Guard's list position for the light.

notes_for_editor: Sources: Lighthouse Friends (community site, facts only; the account of the 1856-1908 structures and the 1969 fire is detailed and dated, but single-source); the Canadian Register's statement of significance (Parks Canada heritage statement); and the Coast Guard list of lights (current characteristics and position). The Parks Canada directory page for this heritage lighthouse (DFHD 14933) returned only the site's notice in this cache, so I cited the Register's reproduction of the same statement; the search index text for the Parks page matches the Register's opening. The 2015 heritage designation and its date (29 May 2015) come from the station record, not from any page I read, so the story does not give a date for it. Possible duplicate: a sibling record ca-nl-belle-isle-south-end-lower (Wikidata Q44452478, coordinates about 51.887, -55.396, heritage events 1990 and 2015) appears to describe this same lighthouse; a merge is for the editor. Do not confuse with the Parks records for 'Belle Isle South West Lower Light' (DFHD 3411) or the 'Lighttower' (DFHD 3408), which are different lights. The keeper roster from Lighthouse Friends appears to be the whole station's list: entries before 1879 (D. Vaughan and the Coltons) predate the lower light and may be keepers of the upper light; the Colton spelling varies (Martin Colton in the roster, Martin Coltin in the 1876 account). Names after about 1960 (Fred Roberts, Clifford Flynn, Fred Osbourne, Abner Budgell) are in the roster as Lighthouse Friends prints them; the story names none of them beyond the roster and gives no injuries or personal details from the 1969 fire. A Chronicling America search for Belle Isle lightning (1876-1877) found no relevant page. No photos added. The Coast Guard's 'Seasonal' note may refer to a seasonal operating period; I have reported it as printed.
